title: HTML Fundamentals
description: Start your web journey by learning the building blocks of every web page. Master HTML tags, elements, attributes, and the essential anatomy of an HTML document.
learningObjectives: Understand what HTML is and how browsers render it
Create a valid HTML document with proper structure
Use opening, closing, and void tags correctly

sections.content: HTML — The Skeleton of the Web

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard language used to create and structure content on the web. Every webpage you have ever visited is built on HTML. Browsers read HTML files and render them into the visual pages you see.
💡 HTML is NOT a programming language — it is a markup language. It describes structure and meaning, not logic.
How Browsers Use HTML

When you open a URL, your browser downloads the HTML file, parses it top-to-bottom, and builds a Document Object Model (DOM) — a tree of all the elements on the page. CSS then styles the DOM, and JavaScript can manipulate it.

Hello, World!

This is my very first web page.
🎯 Save any HTML file with a .html extension, then drag it into your browser — it just works!

exercises.question: What is the purpose of the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration?
options: It tells the browser this is an HTML5 document
It links to a CSS file
exercises.correctAnswer: It tells the browser this is an HTML5 document
exercises.explanation: <!DOCTYPE html> is not an HTML tag but a declaration that tells the browser to render the page in standards mode using HTML5.

sections.content: Anatomy of an HTML Element
An HTML element consists of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. The opening tag marks where the element begins, and the closing tag (with a forward slash) marks where it ends.

This is a paragraph.

Welcome!
Attributes
Attributes provide extra information about elements. They live inside the opening tag as name="value" pairs. Common attributes include id, class, href, src, and alt.

Go to Google

Welcome to my site.
⚠️ Always quote attribute values. While browsers may forgive unquoted values, it is bad practice and can cause bugs.
Void Elements

Some elements have no content and no closing tag. These are called void (or self-closing) elements. Examples include , ,
,
, and .

sections.content: Heading Hierarchy
HTML provides six heading levels from h1 (most important) to h6 (least important). Use only one h1 per page — it represents the main topic. Use h2-h6 to create logical sub-sections.

sections.content: Hyperlinks — The Foundation of the Web
The <a> (anchor) tag creates hyperlinks. The href attribute specifies the destination. Links can point to external URLs, internal pages, section anchors, email addresses, or phone numbers.
Google GitHub About Us Contact Email Me
💡 Always add rel="noopener noreferrer" when using target="_blank" to prevent security vulnerabilities.
Images
The tag embeds images. It is a void element requiring at minimum src (source path) and alt (alternative text). The alt text is critical for accessibility and appears when the image fails to load.
⚠️ Never use an empty alt attribute unless the image is purely decorative (alt=""). Screen readers need meaningful alt text.

sections.content: Unordered Lists

Use <ul> (unordered list) for items with no particular sequence — like a shopping list or a set of features. Each item uses an <li> (list item) tag. Browsers render them with bullet points by default.

• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Cherries
Ordered Lists
Use <ol> (ordered list) when sequence matters — like recipe steps or a tutorial. Items are automatically numbered.

1. Boil water
  2. Add pasta
  3. Cook for 10 minutes
  4. Drain and serve
Nested Lists
Lists can be nested inside each other to create hierarchical structures like outlines or menus.

• Frontend
    • HTML
    • CSS
    • JavaScript
  • Backend
    • Python
    • Node.js
🎯 Use lists for navigation menus — they're semantic, accessible, and easy to style with CSS.
